notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Zechariah 9, drawn from the pages I was able to access. Where a tradition’s voice is missing, I note that honestly.

---

## OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER

**Traditional evangelical outline** (Precept Austin / J. Vernon McGee): Chapters 9–11 form the “First Burden” — prophetic aspects connected with the first coming of Christ. Chapters 12–14 form the “Second Burden” connected with the second coming. Zechariah 9 itself: (a) judgment on the nations vv. 1–8, (b) Israel’s King of Peace vv. 9–10, (c) the King’s mission in relation to Israel vv. 11–17.  
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/zechariah_commentaries

**Gill’s older Baptist reading** sees the whole chapter as treating the conversion of the Gentiles: Syrians (v. 1), Phoenicians (vv. 2–4), Philistines (vv. 5–8), then the coming of Christ and the preaching of the Gospel by the apostles (vv. 9–17).  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-9.html

**The more common modern evangelical reading** (Enduring Word, Ellicott, Constable) sees vv. 1–8 historically fulfilled in Alexander the Great’s conquest (332–331 BC), v. 9 in Christ’s triumphal entry, and v. 10 onward at the second coming/millennium.

---

## VERSE-BY-VERSE NOTES

### v. 1 — *The burden of the word of the LORD against the land of Hadrach and Damascus its resting place…*

- **“Burden”** (Hebrew *massa*): A weighty oracle or pronouncement. Gill notes it can be either sorrowful (judgment) or joyful (good news), and here it is both — judgment on the nations yet good news for the church.  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-9.html

- **Hadrach**: Until the late 19th century this name baffled commentators. Ellicott notes that Assyrian inscriptions (Records of the Past, Vol. V) reveal *Ha-ta-ri-ka* as a town or district near Damascus and Hamath.  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-9.html

- **“Damascus its resting place”**: The judgment/prophecy would settle or “rest” first on Damascus. Ellicott: “the judgments of God should begin at that city.” The LXX reads “his sacrifice” (different vowel pointing).  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-9.html

- **“The eyes of men… are upon the LORD”**: Ellicott renders it “for to the LORD will the eye of man be directed, and that of all the tribes of Israel” — when God’s judgments fall, all eyes turn to Him in wonder. Enduring Word (Guzik) takes it as men watching God’s instrument of judgment (Alexander). Gill interprets it spiritually: when converted, the eyes of men (Gentiles) look to the Lord just as true Israelites do — particularly fulfilled in Paul’s conversion near Damascus (Acts 9).  
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-9/  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-9.html

### v. 2 — *…also against Hamath, which borders it, as well as Tyre and Sidon, though they are very shrewd.*

- **Hamath** bordered Damascus to the north. Gill notes it is called “Hamath the great” (Amos 6:2) and identifies it with Antioch — where the disciples were first called Christians (Acts 11:26).  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-9.html

- **Tyre and Sidon, “though they are very wise”**: An ironic reference to Tyre’s famed wisdom (Ezekiel 28:3). Ellicott says the case of Tyre is decisive for dating: Tyre was never devoured by fire until Alexander in 333 BC (Q. Curtius records he “ordered the houses to be set on fire”).  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-9.html

- Enduring Word: The Assyrians besieged Tyre for 5 years and failed; Nebuchadnezzar tried for 13; Alexander took it in 7 months by building a causeway from the mainland using the rubble of the old city.  
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-9/

### v. 3 — *Tyre has built herself a fortress; she has heaped up silver like dust, and gold like the dirt of the streets.*

- Tyre was built on a rock (its name means “rock”) with walls 150 feet high. Gill: “Tyrus did build herself a strong hold” refers both to its natural and man-made fortifications. Her immense wealth is frequently noted in Scripture (Isaiah 23:2).  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-9.html

### v. 4 — *Behold, the Lord will impoverish her and cast her wealth into the sea, and she will be consumed by fire.*

- **Historical reading** (Enduring Word, Ellicott): Alexander literally threw Tyre’s wealth into the sea when he built his causeway using the rubble, and burned the city. The seven-month siege ended with the island-fortress destroyed.  
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-9/  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-9.html

- **Spiritual reading** (Gill): “The Lord will cast her out” is rendered by the LXX as “the Lord will inherit her” — Tyre’s conversion means she becomes the Lord’s possession. “Smite her power in the sea” = spoiling her carnal strength in which she trusted. “Devoured with fire” = the Spirit’s purging, the fire of the Word, and flames of divine love.  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-9.html

> **Denominational difference noted here**: Gill (older Particular Baptist) reads the judgment language spiritually as conversion; Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic) and Ellicott (Anglican) read it as literal military destruction by Alexander the Great. These two hermeneutical approaches run throughout vv. 1–8.

### v. 5 — *Ashkelon will see and fear; Gaza will writhe in agony, as will Ekron, for her hope will wither. There will cease to be a king in Gaza, and Ashkelon will be uninhabited.*

- **Historical**: The Philistine cities watched Tyre’s destruction and feared as Alexander marched south. Gaza was taken after a five-month siege. Hegesias (a contemporary of Alexander) mentions the “king” of Gaza being brought alive to Alexander.  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-9.html

- **Spiritual** (Gill): Ashkelon sees Tyre’s submission to the Gospel and fears, then itself submits. Gaza is “very sorrowful” at the Gospel’s progress but many submit. Ekron’s “hope” (confidence in its idols) is put to shame. “The king shall perish from Gaza” = the idol Marnes (meaning “lord of man”) worshipped there; when Christianity came, the idol was destroyed and a church built in its place (Jerome). “Ashkelon shall not be inhabited” = not by heathens, but by Christians.  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-9.html

### v. 6 — *A mixed race will occupy Ashdod, and I will cut off the pride of the Philistines.*

- **Historical** (Ellicott): “A bastard” (Hebrew *mamzer*) = a mixed race. Alexander’s policy was to break up nationalities and fuse different peoples.  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-9.html

- **Spiritual** (Gill): “Bastard” (or “stranger,” as the LXX, Syriac, and Arabic render it) = true Christians who are accounted spurious, aliens, the “filth of the world” by the world (1 Cor. 4:13). They would dwell in Ashdod (Azotus, where Philip preached — Acts 8:40).  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-9.html

### v. 7 — *I will remove the blood from their mouths and the abominations from between their teeth… Ekron will be like the Jebusites.*

- **“Blood… abominations”**: Ellicott says these are idolatrous sacrifices — practices involving eating blood and things sacrificed to idols. Gill: they will no longer thirst after blood, breathe out threats against the saints, or eat idol-sacrifices.  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-9.html  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-9.html

- **“Like a clan in Judah… Ekron like the Jebusites”**: Enduring Word explains that David did not wipe out the Jebusites but incorporated them into Israel (Joshua 15:63; 2 Samuel 5:6–9); so the Philistine remnant would be incorporated into God’s people. Gill: the Ekronite convert “shall be as an inhabitant of Jerusalem” (Jebus = Jerusalem, 1 Chronicles 11:4), enjoying all the privileges of the church.  
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-9/  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-9.html

### v. 8 — *But I will camp around My house because of an army… never again will an oppressor overrun My people, for now I keep watch with My own eyes.*

- **Historical** (Enduring Word, Ellicott): When Alexander marched through the Levant towards Egypt, he did not attack Jerusalem. Josephus (*Antiquities* 11.8.4–5) records that the high priest Jaddua had a dream instructing him to open the gates and meet Alexander in priestly garments. Alexander, recognising the high priest from a previous dream-vision, prostrated himself, honoured the Temple, offered sacrifice, and granted the Jews favours.  
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-9/  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-9.html

- **Spiritual** (Gill): “I will encamp about My house” = God’s protection of the church (the house where He dwells) against persecutors and heretics, by angels, ministers, and His own presence. “No oppressor [exactor] shall pass through them any more” = no exactor can demand satisfaction for sin because Christ the Surety has paid it all — the law, divine justice, and Satan cannot exact anything from believers. Gill argues this *cannot* be merely literal because after this prophecy Antiochus, the Romans, and Titus all oppressed the Jews.  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-9.html

> **Key denominational tension**: Gill’s reading is a classic example of a spiritual/Christocentric hermeneutic that sees the entire OT as ultimately fulfilled in the Gospel and the church. The historical-literal school (broadly Dispensational, and also Ellicott) sees primary fulfilment in known historical events and a future millennial consummation for Israel.

### v. 9 — *Rejoice greatly, O Daughter of Zion! … See, your King comes to you, righteous and victorious, humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.*

This is one of the most universally recognised Messianic prophecies in the OT.

- **NT citation**: Matthew 21:5 and John 12:15 quote this verse at Jesus’ triumphal entry. Matthew omits “Rejoice greatly… righteous and having salvation,” which McGee (Precept Austin) says will be fulfilled at the second coming; the rest was fulfilled at the first.  
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/zechariah_commentaries

- **“Righteous and victorious”** (or “just and having salvation”): Ellicott prefers “saved” — the King Himself has been delivered, pointing to Christ’s resurrection (cf. Psalm 2; Acts 2:23–24; Philippians 2:8; Hebrews 5:9).  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-9.html

- **“Humble [or lowly/afflicted]”**: Ellicott renders it “afflicted” (cf. Isaiah 53:4). Ligonier (Reformed) explains: final salvation would not come through a conquering king on a noble horse but “in an unexpected way through what men typically regard as weak and despised.” The donkey is the mount of one coming in peace, not war.  
  — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/king-comes-donkey (via search excerpt)

- **The donkey**: Enduring Word notes the donkey was not a low-status animal but the customary royal mount for peacetime. Kings rode horses into war, donkeys in peace (Judges 5:10; 10:4; 1 Kings 1:33). Clarke adds: “God had commanded the kings of Israel not to multiply horses. Jesus came to fulfill the law. Had he in his title of king rode upon a horse, it would have been a breach of a positive command of God; therefore he rode upon an ass.”  
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-9/

- **“A donkey, a colt, the foal of a donkey”**: This triple description is a Hebrew expression emphasising the animal is purebred — a truly royal mount, not a mule. Constable: “A donkey’s colt was a purebred donkey, one born of a female donkey rather than of a mule.”  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/zechariah-9.html (via search excerpt)

- **Desiring God (Piper, Reformed Baptist)**: Jesus chose the donkey deliberately to show He comes as a gentle peacemaker, not a warrior. “I am meek and lowly in heart; I am approachable … I did not come to condemn but to save.”  
  — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/his-dominion-shall-be-from-sea-to-sea

- **Ellicott** adds: Jesus deliberately fulfilled this not merely to “check a box” but as a *symbolical act* to correct the false notions about the Messiah held by friends and enemies alike. “Any Jew might have fulfilled that part of the prophecy … but could any one have founded an almost universal religion?”  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-9.html

- **Spurgeon** (quoted in Enduring Word): “Brethren, let us be lowly … We must not try to act the lowly part; we must *be* lowly, and then we shall naturally act in a humble manner.”  
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-9/

### v. 10 — *And I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, and the bow of war will be broken. Then He will proclaim peace to the nations. His dominion will extend from sea to sea…*

- **A key interpretive divide**: Most evangelical traditions see a gap between v. 9 (first coming) and v. 10 (second coming / millennium). Enduring Word: “Zechariah 9:9 belongs to the first coming of Jesus, but Zechariah 9:10 is associated with the second coming … the Gospel writers did not go on to quote verse 10, which may indicate that they were conscious of having only a partial fulfillment” (quoting Baldwin).  
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-9/

- **Ligonier (Reformed)** reads v. 10 as the spiritual fruit of Christ’s work: In the day of salvation, Ephraim and Jerusalem would “no longer trust the war horse and chariot” — the salvation achieved by the humble Davidic King would convince God’s people to rest in Him alone rather than in idols of human might (Isa. 31:1; Jer. 42:19).  
  — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/king-comes-donkey (via search excerpt)

- **Ellicott**: “Speak peace” = not only to His own people but to the heathen by setting up His spiritual kingdom among them (cf. Zech. 6:13). “From the River” = the Euphrates (Micah 7:12; Isaiah 7:20). The worldwide reign echoes Psalm 72:8.  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-9.html

- **Gill**: The Messiah’s kingly office is shown — His dominion is very large, universal.  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-9.html

### v. 11 — *As for you, because of the blood of My covenant, I will release your prisoners from the waterless pit.*

- **“Blood of My covenant”**: Several interpretations exist:
  - **Mosaic covenant** (Enduring Word, Ellicott): The blood of Exodus 24:3–8 when Moses sprinkled the people.  
  - **Abrahamic covenant** (Ligonier/Reformed): The covenant God made with Abraham, ratified by the shedding of blood in Genesis 15. “Once more we see the unconditional nature of salvation — God has committed Himself to redeeming His people despite their unfaithfulness.”  
  - **Christ’s blood** (Gill, Biblehub study note): The blood by which the new covenant is confirmed. Biblehub notes Jesus echoes this wording in Matthew 26:28, linking His own blood to release from sin’s prison.  
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-9/  
  — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/king-comes-donkey (via search excerpt)  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-9.html  
  — https://www.biblehub.com/study/chapters/zechariah/9.htm

> **Reformed distinctive**: Ligonier sees “blood of the covenant” as the Abrahamic covenant of grace — unconditional in that God guarantees it, yet conditional in that one enters by repentance and faith. This is a hallmark Reformed covenant-theology reading.

- **“Waterless pit”**: Ellicott says this is Babylon. Enduring Word: a dry cistern — a picture of hopeless captivity (like Joseph in Genesis 37:24 and Jeremiah in Jeremiah 38:6–9). Constable: “God’s people had been in the ‘pit’ of Babylonian exile, but they would find themselves in a worse predicament in the end of the age. From that pit God would again retrieve them.”  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-9.html  
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-9/

### v. 12 — *Return to your stronghold, O prisoners of hope; even today I declare that I will restore to you double.*

- **“Stronghold”**: Enduring Word — both a military fortress and a spiritual fortress in the LORD Himself. Constable: the Stronghold is the LORD Himself (cf. Psalm 18:2; 31:3; 91:2; Nahum 1:7). Gill: Christ Himself is the stronghold.  
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-9/

- **“Prisoners of hope”**: Ellicott — those still in Babylon are “prisoners” yet “of hope” because glorious promises are theirs if they accept them.  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-9.html

- **“Restore double”**: Ellicott — recompense for sufferings (Isaiah 61:7). Constable: a double restoration pictures a *complete* restoration (metonymy; cf. Job 42:10–13; Isaiah 40:2).  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-9.html

### v. 13 — *For I will bend Judah as My bow and fit it with Ephraim. I will rouse your sons, O Zion, against the sons of Greece…*

- **Historical fulfilment**: Ellicott says this was “signally fulfilled in the triumphs of the Maccabees over the Grecian rulers of Syria (B.C. 167–130).” Judah = the bow, Ephraim = the arrow. The reunion of the two kingdoms under one King fulfills Ezekiel 37:16–17.  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-9.html

- **Enduring Word** agrees on partial Maccabean fulfilment but sees ultimate fulfilment yet future.  
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-9/

- **Spiritual reading** (Gill): The apostles are represented as military men — Judah the bow, Ephraim the arrow — accoutered for spiritual warfare through the preaching of the Gospel.  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-9.html

### v. 14 — *Then the LORD will appear over them, and His arrow will go forth like lightning. The Lord GOD will sound the ram’s horn and advance in the whirlwinds of the south.*

- Ellicott: “Shall be seen over them” = on their behalf He manifests Himself. The theophany language — lightning as His arrows, thunder as His war-trumpet, the south wind as the fury of His might — depicts the LORD as divine warrior.  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-9.html

- Enduring Word: “The LORD Himself leads the battle … Jesus alone carries out the biblical holy war, and never His people” — contrasting biblical holy war with Islamic Jihad.  
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-9/

### v. 15 — *The LORD of Hosts will shield them. They will destroy and conquer with slingstones; they will drink and roar as with wine… filled like sprinkling bowls, drenched like the corners of the altar.*

- **“Slingstones”**: Ellicott — “trample on sling stones” (i.e., they will charge valiantly over the enemy’s projectiles). Gill — the slingstones represent the Gospel or the apostles’ preaching, which brings down the enemies of God.  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-9.html  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-9.html

- **“Drink and roar as with wine”**: Gill takes this as being filled with the Spirit (cf. Ephesians 5:18). Ellicott takes it more literally as the fury of battle — devouring the enemy like a lion (Numbers 23:24).

- **“Filled like sprinkling bowls… corners of the altar”**: Ellicott — filled with the blood of enemies, like the sacrificial bowls used to catch and sprinkle blood. Gill — filled with the Spirit, wholly consecrated to God like the altar vessels.  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-9.html

### v. 16 — *On that day the LORD their God will save them as the flock of His people; for like jewels in a crown they will sparkle over His land.*

- Ellicott notes this is the first introduction of the “flock” image that dominates the following chapters (Zechariah 10–11).  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-9.html

- Enduring Word: “The LORD their God will save them in that day. This is God’s battle, not the battle of men.”  
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-9/

### v. 17 — *How lovely they will be, and how beautiful! Grain will make the young men flourish, and new wine, the young women.*

- Enduring Word: Grain and new wine are pictures of millennial prosperity and blessing (cf. Hosea 2:21–22; Joel 2:19).  
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-9/

- Ellicott: “Goodness” = goodliness (Hosea 10:11). “Make to grow numerously” (cf. Psalm 72:16).  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-9.html

- Gill concludes the chapter with an exclamation “wondering at the grace and glory of Christ, and expressing the satisfying provisions of his house.”  
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-9.html

## DENOMINATIONAL DIFFERENCES OBSERVED

### 1. Historical-Literal vs. Spiritual/Ecclesiological reading of vv. 1–8

| Approach | Representatives | Reading |
|----------|----------------|---------|
| **Historical-literal** | Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic), Ellicott (Anglican), Constable (Dispensational) | vv. 1–8 fulfilled by Alexander the Great’s conquest, with Jerusalem miraculously spared |
| **Spiritual/Christocentric** | Gill (older Particular Baptist) | The whole passage describes Gentile conversion — the cities that fall to the Gospel, idols abolished, and converts incorporated into the church |

### 2. “Blood of the covenant” (v. 11)

| Tradition | Identification |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Reformed / Covenant Theology** (Ligonier) | The Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 15), emphasising unconditional election |
| **Dispensational / Evangelical** (Enduring Word, Ellicott, Constable) | The Mosaic covenant (Exodus 24:3–8) |
| **Christocentric** (Gill, Biblehub study note) | The new covenant in Christ’s blood (Matthew 26:28) |

### 3. The relationship between v. 9 and v. 10

| View | Reading |
|------|---------|
| **Dispensational** (McGee, Constable, Enduring Word) | v. 9 = first coming (triumphal entry); v. 10 = second coming / millennium. The NT writers deliberately quote only v. 9, recognising partial fulfilment. |
| **Reformed / Amillennial-leaning** (Ligonier, some readings) | Both v. 9 and v. 10 describe aspects of Christ’s present spiritual reign — peace proclaimed to the nations through the Gospel, universal dominion through the church. |

### 4. vv. 13–17: Maccabean or eschatological?

| View | Reading |
|------|---------|
| **Ellicott** (and many older commentators) | vv. 11–17 fulfilled in the Maccabean wars (167–130 BC) |
| **Dispensational / Premillennial** (McGee, Enduring Word) | Partial Maccabean fulfilment, ultimate fulfilment at Christ’s return |
| **Spiritual** (Gill) | Fulfilled in apostolic preaching and the spread of the church |
